title: How to win the World Memory Championship

paragraphs.text: Last August, 34 contestants gathered at the World Memory Championships held at Oxford University. In timed trials, they were challenged to memorise rows of 40-digit numbers, recall the names of 110 people after looking at their photographs and memorise the sequence of a shuffled pack of playing cards. No-one has ever managed this last feat in under 30 seconds and that number has become the target for ‘mental athletes’. Even so, most contestants in the memory championships claim to have just average memories and scientific testing confirms that this isn’t false modesty. Their feats are based on tricks that capitalise on how the human brain encodes information. We all have the potential to perform just as well if we are taught certain strategies.

Psychologists Elizabeth Valentine and John Wilding recently teamed up with Eleanor Maguire, a neuroscientist at University College London, to study eight of those contestants. They wondered if their brains were different in some way. They put the contestants and a group of control subjects into an MRI* machine and asked them to perform several different memory tests while their brains were being scanned. When it came to memorising sequences of three-digit numbers, the difference between the subjects was, as anticipated, immense. However, when they were shown photographs of magnified snowflakes, images that the contestants had never tried to memorise before, the champions did no better than the control group. When the brain scans were analysed, they showed the champions were activating some brain regions that were different from those the control subjects were using. These regions are known to be involved in visual memory and spatial navigation.

This makes sense when you listen to Ed Cooke, a 23-year-old cognitive science graduate and championship contestant, explain his method. He has memorised a specific person, verb and object that he associated with each card in the deck, and when he commits a shuffled deck to memory, he does it three cards at a time. Every three-card group then forms a single image of a person doing something to an object. He takes the person from the first card, the verb from the second and the object from the third.

Yet even meaningful information is hard to remember when there’s much of it. That’s why memorisers place their images along an imaginary path and why the brain scans of the contestants showed activation in the brain regions associated with visual imagery and navigation in space. Cooke also places images along a path he knows well and when it is time to recall the cards, he takes a mental walk along it and translates the images into cards. This technique, known as the loci method, reportedly originated in 477 BC with the Greek poet Simonides. He was able to reconstruct a long guest list by closing his eyes and recalling each individual around the dinner table. He had discovered that our brains are exceptionally good at remembering images and spatial information. Evolutionary psychologists have offered a credible explanation: our ancestors found it important to remember where they found their last meal or the way back to shelter. In other words, these skills were really vital.

After Simonides’s discovery, the loci method became popular across classical Greece and Rome as a trick for memorising speeches, to make their delivery appear more spontaneous to the audience. Before books, the art of memory was considered a basic of classical education, on a par with grammar and logic. Today external aids supplant natural memory: Palm Pilots track schedules, cell phones store phone numbers, and internet searches turn up a bonanza of information. About the only place where you’ll find people still using the loci method is at the championships.

But is there a form of innately superior memory? Valentine and Wilding think so. They divide people with superior memories into two classes — strategists and naturals. The former employ techniques that convert meaningless information into a form the brain can organise and retain, but they tend to be exceptional at memorising only a few types of things. Naturals, on the other hand, show strong memory across a wide variety of tasks and tend to have an easier time holding on to those memories. Apparently, the most famous ‘natural’ was the 20th-century Russian journalist S V Shereshevski, whose memory seemed to have limitless capacity. He could recite strings of numbers learnt decades earlier and recite pages and pages of poetry. He was one of the rare people born with synesthesia, meaning that his senses became intertwined. For example, every number may be associated with a colour or every word with a taste. Synesthetic reactions evoke a response in more areas of the brain, making memory easier. Nevertheless, other research casts doubt on Valentine’s and Wilding’s theories.

K Anders Ericsson, a Swedish-born psychologist at Florida State University, thinks anyone can acquire Shereshevski’s skills. He cites an experiment with an undergraduate who was paid to take a test of memory called the digit span for one hour a day, three days a week. When he started, he could merely hold seven digits in his head at any given time. But after 250 hours of testing, he stretched to 80. He had developed a strategy for remembering, based on his experience as a professional runner. He associated random numbers with track times. For example, 3,492 was remembered as “three minutes and 49 point 2 seconds, near world-record time.’ This study led Ericsson to believe that innately superior memory doesn’t exist. After reviewing original case studies of naturals, he found that exceptional memorisers were using techniques — sometimes without realising it — and lots of practice.
